uncited: Isosurface extraction generates an explicit polygonal mesh representing the surface where a scalar field equals a specific threshold (isovalue) from volumetric data.
It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures or boundaries within volumetric data by approximating the implicit surface $f(x,y,z) = I$.
What sets this family apart from direct volume rendering is that it produces an explicit geometric representation (mesh) rather than a rasterized image.
All isosurface extraction algorithms operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values at its vertices.
The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells and evaluating the scalar field at cell vertices or edges.
For cubic grids, vertex values are compared against the isovalue to determine a topological configuration (e.g., a 256-case index).
For tetrahedral or hybrid grids, the method identifies edges where the scalar field changes sign.
Intersection points are computed using inverse linear interpolation for the parameter and linear interpolation for 3D coordinates: $t = (I - f_a) / (f_b - f_a)$ and $P = V_a + t(V_b - V_a)$.
The intersection points are then connected to form primitives (triangles, quads, or polygons).
Adjacent cell primitives are merged into a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates.
